rubric: Attributes much of PC1's variance to the two capability anchors, which are strongly intercorrelated and load heavily.
Notes that the 0.22 median concerns only benchmark-to-benchmark pairs, not anchor pairs.

items.question: In the metric sensitivity analysis, why does R-Judge load most strongly on PC1 under balanced accuracy (−0.86) rather than under specificity (−0.71) or recall (−0.14)?
items.answer: PC1 is aligned with the capability anchors. Of the R-Judge metrics, balanced accuracy is among the most strongly capability-correlated (+0.71 with MMLU), whereas specificity is +0.16 and recall +0.40. Balanced accuracy also combines both error types, so it captures the cluster-aligned discrimination signal that neither component carries alone.
rubric: Links the PC1 loading to the metric's correlation with capability, since PC1 is aligned with the anchors.
Notes that balanced accuracy is strongly capability-correlated (+0.71 MMLU) while specificity (+0.16) and recall (+0.40) are much weaker.

items.question: Why does averaging over three jailbreak templates leave no model at the ceiling, when AIM alone leaves 11 of 22 models refusing every request?
items.answer: A model reaches the ceiling of the averaged score only if it refuses every prompt under all three templates. The models that fully refuse AIM must comply with at least some prompts under refusal-suppression or prefix-injection, so their averages fall below the maximum. This restores between-model variance, which also lets the AgentHarm partial rise from +0.50 to +0.72.
rubric: Explains that a ceiling on the average would require full refusal under every template, and the AIM-ceiling models comply on some prompts under the other templates.
Notes that this restores variance among models (optionally linked to the higher partial).

items.question: R-Judge has 21 valid models and the anchor panel has 21 models. Why are the RQ2 capability correlations computed at n = 20?
items.answer: The two 21-model panels drop different models. R-Judge excludes Qwen3-32B for unparseable output, and the anchor panel excludes DeepSeek-R1 for unstable GPQA generation. Their intersection is therefore 20 models.
rubric: Identifies that the two panels exclude different models (Qwen3-32B from R-Judge, DeepSeek-R1 from the anchors).
Concludes that the overlap is 20.

items.question: The paper warns that within-model uncertainty does not support every pairwise model difference. Why can it nonetheless treat the misalignment safety gap among o3-mini (0.99), Grok-4.3 (0.70) and DeepSeek-V3 (0.19) at composite ≈ 0.8 as real?
items.answer: The worst-case within-model SE for misalignment is about 5 points. These gaps are about 29 and 80 points, many times that SE. The caveat applies only to close pairs, not to differences this large.
rubric: Says the gaps are much larger than the misalignment SE (max ≈ 5 points).
Notes that the pairwise caveat applies only to models with close scores.

items.question: Claude-3-Haiku looks like a blanket refuser: AgentHarm safety 0.81, R-Judge specificity 0.40, and 60% over-refusal on XSTest. Why does the panel-level AgentHarm–over-refusal partial nonetheless come out at −0.01?
items.answer: A rank correlation over 17 models is not driven by one extreme case. Most models over-refuse at 15% or less, and across them AgentHarm rank does not track over-refusal rank. Some high-AgentHarm models, such as o3-mini, over-refuse only moderately. Controlling capability further removes shared variance, so one cautious model does not create a panel association.
rubric: Says a single model cannot drive a Spearman correlation over 17 models.
Notes that across the rest of the panel AgentHarm safety does not line up with over-refusal (most models ≤15%).

items.question: Would capability's raw correlations with the three held-out criteria (Table 2, top row) be unchanged if the capability composite were replaced by the anchors' first principal component score?
items.answer: Yes. These are Spearman correlations, which depend only on model ordering. The paper states that the composite's ordering is identical to the anchors' first principal component.
rubric: Says yes, they would be unchanged.
Explains that Spearman uses only ranks and the composite's ordering matches the anchors' PC1.

items.question: Would capability's raw correlations with the three held-out criteria (Table 2, top row) necessarily be unchanged if the capability composite were replaced by GPQA alone?
items.answer: No. GPQA orders the models differently from the composite. The RQ2 results show this: MMLU and GPQA give different correlations with the same R-Judge metrics (e.g., +0.71 vs +0.49 for balanced accuracy). A different ordering can change Spearman correlations.
rubric: Says no, they could change.
Explains that GPQA's ordering differs from the composite's, evidenced by MMLU and GPQA giving different correlations with the same R-Judge metric.

items.question: If every audited benchmark score were re-expressed as log-odds, keeping each model's ordering, would the full-panel R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm-safety correlation of +0.02 change?
items.answer: No. All association tests use Spearman correlations, which are invariant to monotone transformations that preserve model order.
rubric: Says it would not change.
Cites the rank-based (Spearman) correlation's invariance to order-preserving transforms.

items.question: If every audited benchmark score were re-expressed as log-odds, keeping each model's ordering, would the corroborative PCA's PC1 share of 48.7% necessarily stay the same?
items.answer: No. The PCA runs on the Pearson correlation matrix of standardized scores, which depends on actual values rather than ranks alone. The paper shows that switching to a rank-based PCA already moves PC1 from 48.7% to 40.8%.
rubric: Says it would not necessarily stay the same.
Explains that the PCA uses Pearson correlations, which are sensitive to value transforms, citing the Pearson vs Spearman shift (48.7% vs 40.8%).

items.question: If a fourth held-out criterion were added, making the Bonferroni family 12 partial tests, would the AgentHarm→jailbreak partial still survive correction?
items.answer: Yes. The corrected α would be about 0.05/12 ≈ 0.004, and the AgentHarm→jailbreak partial has p < 0.001.
rubric: Says yes, it survives.
Compares p < 0.001 with the corrected α of about 0.004.

items.question: If a fourth held-out criterion were added, making the Bonferroni family 12 partial tests, would the InjecAgent–misalignment partial survive correction?
items.answer: No. Its p-value is about 0.05–0.09, far above a corrected α of about 0.004. It already fails at the nine-test α of 0.006.
rubric: Says no, it does not survive.
Compares p ≈ 0.05–0.09 with the corrected α of about 0.004 (or notes it already fails at 0.006).

items.question: After dropping near-ceiling Anthropic, would the capability-adjusted organization-group difference on misalignment be significant at α = 0.01?
items.answer: No. Without Anthropic, the misalignment group test gives p = 0.018, which is significant at 0.05 but not at 0.01.
rubric: Says no.

items.question: After dropping near-ceiling Anthropic, would the capability-adjusted organization-group difference on jailbreak be significant at α = 0.01?
items.answer: Yes. Without Anthropic, the jailbreak group test gives p < 0.001, with ε² = 0.54.
rubric: Says yes.
Cites p < 0.001 (ε² = 0.54) after dropping Anthropic.

items.question: On the expanded panel, capability correlates +0.34 with jailbreak safety. Can a deployer use MMLU/GPQA scores to screen high-capability candidates for jailbreak safety?
items.answer: No, not reliably. Among high-capability models jailbreak safety spans roughly 0.09 to 0.99 (Mistral-Large 0.09, DeepSeek-V3 0.37, Anthropic/OpenAI 0.98–0.99). Organization groups differ strongly after capability adjustment (ε² = 0.57). The deployer would need to measure jailbreak safety directly.
rubric: Says capability anchors are not a reliable screen.
Cites the near-full spread of jailbreak safety among high-capability models, or the large capability-adjusted organization differences (ε² = 0.57).

items.question: A deployer requires InjecAgent robustness ≥ 0.90 and AgentHarm safety ≥ 0.60. Using Table 1, which models qualify, and what does this show about using InjecAgent as a proxy for AgentHarm?
items.answer: Only Qwen-2.5-72B qualifies (0.92 / 0.60). The other models with InjecAgent ≥ 0.90 have much lower AgentHarm safety: GPT-4.1-nano 0.94 / 0.42 and GPT-4o 0.90 / 0.47. Top injection robustness does not imply refusal of harmful tasks, so InjecAgent cannot stand in for AgentHarm.
rubric: Identifies Qwen-2.5-72B as the only qualifying model.
Notes that other top-InjecAgent models (e.g., GPT-4.1-nano, GPT-4o) score low on AgentHarm, so one benchmark is not a proxy for the other.

items.question: A team wants to validate a new prompt-injection benchmark by correlating it with AgentDojo. Based on the paper, which AgentDojo score should it use, and what else should it ensure?
items.answer: It should use AgentDojo's security score rather than its utility score. AgentDojo is environment-scored for both, and blinded coders read it as task success 4/7 times, so utility-laden scores would blend in task ability. The team should also run it on far more than five models, since the paper's own convergent control was inconclusive at n = 5.
rubric: Recommends the security component rather than utility or task success.
Cites that AgentDojo blends utility scoring (coders read it as task success 4/7).
Says the panel must be much larger than n = 5.

items.question: A team computing split-half consistency for a multi-template jailbreak suite plans to resample individual template-prompt pairs as independent items. What does the paper's approach suggest instead, and why?
items.answer: It should resample by base prompt, as the paper does. The three templates applied to the same base prompt are dependent, so treating each template-prompt pair as independent would overstate the number of independent items and overstate consistency.
rubric: Recommends resampling by base prompt.
Explains that template variants of the same prompt are dependent, so pair-level resampling would overstate precision or consistency.

items.question: A team has two models from each of three organizations and wants to claim that one organization's models are safer at matched capability. What does the paper's analysis suggest about this plan?
items.answer: The plan is not adequate. The paper's group comparison used only organizations with at least three models and rested on a permutation test whose calibration it checked by simulation. Even then it calls the result observational, because the static composite may miss agentic capability. Two models per organization cannot support a matched-capability organizational claim, let alone a causal one.
rubric: Says the plan is inadequate or the claim unsupported.
Cites the paper's ≥3-models-per-group requirement or the small-n and few-cluster limits.
Notes that even the paper's result is observational, because the static composite may miss agentic ability.

items.question: A newly released model has a provider-reported GPQA score but no MMLU result from the paper's harness. How should a team running the paper's capability-controlled analyses handle it?
items.answer: The team should measure both anchors under the uniform protocol: the fixed 500-item MMLU subset and GPQA-Diamond with chain-of-thought, through the same harness. If that is not possible, the model should be excluded from capability-controlled analyses, as the paper did with GLM-4.5 and DeepSeek-R1. Mixing in provider numbers is what made the composite fail its positive control (MMLU loading 0.42).
rubric: Says to measure both anchors under the same protocol, or else exclude the model from capability-controlled analyses.
Justifies this with the failed positive control on provider-reported anchors or the paper's exclusion of models lacking the anchor pair.

items.question: If re-measuring MMLU and GPQA under the uniform protocol had flipped the sign of the capability–misalignment correlation relative to the provider-reported anchors, which result would lose support?
items.answer: The capability crossover would lose support. Its misalignment arm would then depend on where the anchor numbers came from rather than on model behavior. The paper's robustness argument relies on every RQ2/RQ3 sign being unchanged by harmonization.
rubric: Names the capability crossover (task success vs misalignment), or the negative capability–misalignment correlation.
Explains that the result would become sensitive to anchor provenance, contradicting the reported unchanged signs.

items.question: If AgentHarm's jailbreak-over-misalignment selectivity test had given p = 0.01 under organization resampling, how would the paper's characterization of the AgentHarm–jailbreak result change?
items.answer: The claim that AgentHarm is selective for jailbreak over misalignment would no longer be borderline, because it would survive the stricter organization-level resampling. The +0.72 would still partly reflect convergent measurement of harmful compliance, but the outcome-specificity claim the paper now leaves open would gain firm support.
rubric: Says the selectivity claim would become firm rather than borderline.
Notes that the convergent-validity overlap (both measure harmful compliance) would still apply.

items.question: If the blackmail and leaking halves of the misalignment criterion had agreed at only about Spearman–Brown 0.1, which results would lose support even though the independent grader agrees at ρ = 0.97?
items.answer: Results treating misalignment safety as one coherent outcome would be undermined. These include the misalignment arm of the capability crossover, the expanded-panel misalignment update, and the exploratory R-Judge/InjecAgent associations. Grader agreement shows only that scoring is consistent, not that the two scenarios measure the same propensity.
rubric: Names the misalignment-based results: the crossover's misalignment arm and/or the R-Judge/InjecAgent associations or the expansion result.
Explains that grader agreement addresses scoring, not whether the scenarios measure one construct.

items.question: If R-Judge specificity, InjecAgent robustness and AgentHarm safety had ordered the 18 common-panel models almost identically, which of the paper's RQ1 results would lose its basis?
items.answer: The paper's firmest, correlation-free RQ1 result would lose its basis: the ranking disagreement in Table 1. That result supports the claim that safety rank is benchmark-dependent and that scores cannot be quoted interchangeably.
rubric: Names the Table 1 ranking disagreement, the firm descriptive RQ1 result.
Links it to the conclusion that the benchmarks are not interchangeable and safety rank is benchmark-dependent.

items.question: If the independent jailbreak judge had agreed with the original StrongREJECT grader only at ρ ≈ 0.5 instead of 0.98, which results would lose robustness support?
items.answer: The AgentHarm–jailbreak partial (+0.72) would lose its grader-robustness support. So would the jailbreak results on the expanded panel: the capability–jailbreak correlation of +0.34 and the organization-group differences on jailbreak. These results would then depend on the choice of judge.
rubric: Names the AgentHarm–jailbreak association.
Also names at least one expanded-panel jailbreak result (capability +0.34 or organization differences), or states that the results would become judge-dependent.

items.question: If the six-model BFCL pilot had produced a capability ranking consistent with the static anchors, which caveat on the organization-group finding could the paper have begun to address?
items.answer: It could have begun to address the caveat that the static MMLU/GPQA composite may miss agentic ability. A validated agentic anchor would let capability-adjusted organization differences be checked against agentic capability, reducing the chance that unmeasured agentic ability shows up as an organization effect.
rubric: Names the caveat that the static composite may miss agentic capability.
Explains that a validated agentic anchor would allow adjusting for it, so organization differences are less likely to be unmeasured capability.

items.question: Does the paper show that the capability crossover (Δ = −1.00) weakened on the expanded 41-model panel? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. τ² task success was not re-collected for the expansion, so the interaction Δ could not be recomputed. Only the misalignment arm was updated, and its change is itself not significant.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that τ² was not re-collected, so only the misalignment correlation, not Δ, was updated.

items.question: Does the paper show that R-Judge, under some choice of metric, predicts jailbreak safety beyond capability? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Across all four R-Judge metrics the capability-controlled jailbreak partials are small and negative (−0.05 to −0.20), and the paper describes the jailbreak null as stable across metrics.
rubric: Answers contradicted (or not supported, with the data pointing to no association).
Cites the small negative partials under every metric (−0.05 to −0.20).

items.question: Does the paper show that R-Judge clusters with capability and InjecAgent on PC1 whichever R-Judge metric is used? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. R-Judge loads strongly under specificity, balanced accuracy and F1 (−0.71, −0.86, −0.75), but only −0.14 under recall. Its membership in the cluster therefore depends on the metric.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites the weak recall loading (−0.14) against strong loadings for the other metrics.

items.question: Does the paper show that the Table 1 ranking disagreement is free of grader or judge effects? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The internal-consistency analysis rules out item-sampling error but does not address judge choice. Rescoring AgentHarm refusals with a different judge agreed only at ρ = 0.69, so AgentHarm's model positions show some judge dependence, even though the AgentHarm–jailbreak partial barely moved.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that split-half and rank stability address item sampling, not graders.
Cites the AgentHarm judge-swap agreement of 0.69.

items.question: Does the paper show that InjecAgent and AgentHarm headline scores can likewise be matched by a constant degenerate policy? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Observation 1 concerns binary trace-judgment benchmarks scored by F1, demonstrated on R-Judge. InjecAgent is scored as attack success and AgentHarm as harmful compliance, and the paper does not analyze constant-policy baselines for them.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that Observation 1 applies to F1-scored binary trace judgment (R-Judge), while the other benchmarks use different metrics that the paper does not analyze this way.

items.question: Does the paper show that high R-Judge specificity reflects a general permissive tendency to rarely flag or refuse anything? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper notes only that specificity can be inflated by rarely flagging anything. Its XSTest check does not support general permissiveness: specificity relates +0.15 (n.s.) to over-refusal, the opposite direction, and the highest-specificity model, o3-mini, over-refuses 30% of benign prompts. The check is low-powered, so it settles nothing either way.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Cites the XSTest evidence: specificity's weak positive (+0.15, n.s.) relation with over-refusal, or o3-mini's 30% over-refusal.
Notes that the check is low-powered or non-significant.

items.question: On the original 21-model panel, o3-mini is described as a capable exception on misalignment safety. If o3-mini were dropped, would the capability–misalignment correlation likely move further from zero or closer to zero, and why?
items.answer: It would likely become more negative, moving further from zero. In Table 1, o3-mini has the highest capability (GPQA 77.2), yet it blackmails or leaks only 1% of the time. A high-capability, high-safety point runs against the negative trend, so removing it should strengthen that trend.
rubric: Says the correlation would likely become more negative (stronger, further from zero).
Reason: o3-mini pairs top capability with near-perfect misalignment safety (about 1% misbehavior), which works against the negative capability–safety trend.

items.question: Does the capability-adjusted organization-group result on the expanded panel tell us anything about developers that contribute only one or two models to that panel?
items.answer: No. The group test includes only the seven organizations with at least three models, for a total of n = 33. The other 8 of the 41 models, from the remaining five organizations, are not part of the comparison, so their capability-adjusted standing is untested.
rubric: Says no, the result does not cover such developers.
Reason: the test is limited to groups with at least 3 models (total n = 33), which leaves about 8 models from five smaller organizations out of the comparison.

items.question: If the post-hoc three-scenario battery (adding murder) replaced blackmail+leaking as the misalignment criterion, would AgentHarm's selectivity for jailbreak over misalignment likely hold up?
items.answer: It would likely weaken substantially. AgentHarm forecasts the battery at about +0.43, compared with +0.13 on the primary criterion. Against its +0.72 jailbreak partial, the gap would therefore shrink from about 0.59 to about 0.29, and the selectivity test is already borderline. The cause is that murder is a severe overt harm, which harm-compliance measures predict.
rubric: Says selectivity would likely weaken or fail.

Reason: AgentHarm's association with the battery (about +0.43) is far above its +0.13 with the primary criterion, so the gap to +0.72 shrinks to roughly 0.3, starting from a test that is already borderline.
Mentions that murder is a severe harm that harm-compliance forecasts, which dilutes construct specificity.

items.question: Could R-Judge F1 sampling error alone overturn the finding that the always-unsafe baseline outranks five discriminating models?
items.answer: No. The five models score 0.30–0.57, at least 0.12 below the baseline's 0.690. The worst-case bootstrap SE of R-Judge F1 is about 3.0 points (0.03), so every gap is at least about four times the worst-case SE. The baseline itself is an exact closed form with no sampling error.
rubric: Says no, sampling error cannot overturn it.
Reason: the gaps (at least about 0.12) are several times the worst-case F1 SE of about 0.03 from the within-model uncertainty analysis.

items.question: Suppose R-Judge were run on a completely different panel, such as the 2026 expansion models. Which part of the RQ4 finding could change and which could not?
items.answer: The baseline's F1 of 0.690 could not change, because it depends only on the item base rate π = 0.527 via 2π/(1+π). How many models fall below it, the 'five', and how narrowly the top-specificity model beats it could both change, since those depend on which models are evaluated.
rubric: Says the constant baseline's F1 (0.690) is fixed regardless of panel because it depends only on the items' unsafe share.
Says the number of models outranked, and the margins of specific models, are panel-dependent and could change.

items.question: Does the full-panel R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm correlation of +0.02 at n = 18 rule out a modest true trade-off, say ρ ≈ −0.3?
items.answer: No. At n = 18 the paper's minimum detectable effect at 80% power is 0.62, and power to detect even 0.4 is only about 0.35. A true −0.3 relationship would usually go undetected. The +0.02 shows that the strong −0.64 trade-off does not persist, not that the relationship is exactly zero.
rubric: Says no, it cannot rule out a modest trade-off.
Reason: power at n = 18 is low (minimum detectable effect 0.62; power about 0.35 for ρ = 0.4), so effects around 0.3 are undetectable.

items.question: Why is AgentHarm's selectivity contrast Δ = +0.59, rather than the difference between its Table 2 partials (+0.72 jailbreak, +0.16 misalignment)?
items.answer: The selectivity test is run on the paired n = 19 panel. There, AgentHarm's misalignment partial is +0.13, and 0.72 − 0.13 = 0.59. Table 2's +0.16 comes from the common n = 18 panel.
rubric: Says the test uses a different (paired n = 19) panel on which the misalignment partial is +0.13.
Shows that 0.72 − 0.13 = 0.59, whereas +0.16 belongs to the n = 18 common panel.

items.question: Why is the capability crossover Δ = −1.00 rather than the −1.04 implied by Table 2's capability row (+0.60 for τ², −0.44 for misalignment)?
items.answer: The interaction is computed on the paired n = 20 panel, the models with τ² scores. On that panel the capability–misalignment correlation is −0.41, and −0.41 − 0.60 ≈ −1.00. The −0.44 is from the full 21-model misalignment panel.
rubric: Says the crossover uses the paired n = 20 panel, where the misalignment correlation is −0.41.
Shows that the difference −0.41 − 0.60 is about −1.00, while −0.44 belongs to the n = 21 panel.

items.question: Why is capability's correlation with jailbreak safety on the original panel computed at n = 21, when the jailbreak criterion itself covers 22 models?
items.answer: Capability analyses need MMLU/GPQA anchors. DeepSeek-R1 was excluded from the 21-model anchor panel because its long-form GPQA generation was unstable. It has a jailbreak score but no capability composite, so it drops out.
rubric: Identifies DeepSeek-R1 as the model without capability anchors.
Reason: it was excluded from the anchor panel for unstable GPQA generation, so it cannot enter capability-based correlations.

items.question: Why does the organization-group test on the expanded panel use a total of n = 33 rather than the 40–41 models scored on the criteria?
items.answer: The group comparison includes only organizations with at least three anchored models. Seven of the 12 organizations qualify. The roughly 8 models from the other five organizations, each with only one or two models, are left out.
rubric: Says the test is restricted to organizations contributing at least three models (seven groups).
Says models from the remaining smaller organizations (about 8 models across five organizations) are excluded.

items.question: Why does inter-coder agreement drop from Krippendorff's α = 0.825 in the four-benchmark coding to 0.61 in the six-target coding with a distractor, even though AgentHarm and the jailbreak criterion stay unanimous?
items.answer: The second round adds a third category and targets that are genuinely contested. AgentDojo, which is utility-scored, is read as task success by 4 of 7 coders, and InjecAgent splits 5/7. The added misalignment criterion is also ambiguous, since avoiding a harmful action can be read as recognition or as blocking. The disagreement concentrates on these targets, not on the clean AgentHarm/jailbreak/R-Judge assignments.
rubric: Attributes the drop to contested targets and the extra category, not to the AgentHarm/jailbreak assignments.
Names at least one specific source, such as AgentDojo read as task success (4/7) because it is utility-scored, InjecAgent's 5/7 split, or the ambiguous misalignment criterion.

items.question: R-Judge specificity and InjecAgent robustness load in the same direction as the capability anchors on PC1. Why do they nonetheless add nothing to τ² task-success prediction once capability is controlled?
items.answer: Whatever τ²-relevant signal they carry is mostly the part they share with capability, and partialling out the composite removes it. Their remaining benchmark-specific variance is unrelated to task success (partials −0.09 and +0.16, n.s.).
rubric: Says their τ²-relevant variance overlaps with capability and is removed by the partial correlation.
Notes that the residual partials are small and non-significant (about −0.09 and +0.16).

items.question: Prior work reports cross-benchmark rank concordance near 0.10 from a twelve-model check. Based on this paper's findings, how much weight should a reader put on that specific value?
items.answer: The qualitative message, that agreement is weak, is consistent with this paper's median between-benchmark correlation of 0.22 at n = 18. The exact value at about 12 models should be treated as imprecise. This paper shows small panels produce large spurious correlations: a quarter of size-7 subsets reach |ρ| ≥ 0.5 around a near-zero value. An estimate at n ≈ 12 could be far from the population value.
rubric: Says the low-agreement conclusion is broadly consistent with this paper (median correlation about 0.22), but the precise value is unreliable.
Reason: the paper's small-panel evidence (for example, about 25% of size-7 subsets reaching |ρ| ≥ 0.5) shows correlations at around a dozen models are highly variable.

items.question: A monitor benchmark reports miss rate and false-alarm rate separately, rather than a single F1. Could a policy that flags every case exploit it the way the always-unsafe policy exploits R-Judge F1?
items.answer: No. Flagging everything gives a 0% miss rate but a 100% false-alarm rate, which is plainly visible. F1 hides this because it gives no credit for true negatives. Two-sided reporting exposes the behavior that F1 conceals.
rubric: Says no, the degenerate policy would be exposed.
Reason: its false-alarm rate would be 100%, and that true-negative failure is exactly what F1 ignores.

items.question: A team plans to validate a new agent-safety benchmark against a single held-out criterion. Based on the RQ3 results for AgentHarm, what risk does this plan carry?
items.answer: Its verdict could hinge on which criterion is chosen. AgentHarm would look strongly valid against three-template jailbreak safety (+0.72). Against misalignment it would look weak (+0.16), and against τ² task success it would look like it adds nothing beyond capability (−0.23). A single criterion can therefore give an unrepresentative picture, so several distinct outcomes should be tested.
rubric: Says the conclusion would depend on which criterion was picked, and could be misleading either way.
Supports this with AgentHarm's differing partials across jailbreak (+0.72), misalignment (+0.16) and τ² (−0.23).

items.question: A deployer must choose between o3-mini and DeepSeek-V3, which have similar capability composites (about 0.8) on the expanded panel, and cares about agentic misalignment. Which should it prefer, and could capability scores have told it this?
items.answer: It should prefer o3-mini, whose misalignment safety is 0.99 against DeepSeek-V3's 0.19. DeepSeek-V3 is also weak on jailbreak (0.37). Capability could not have told it this: both models sit at about the same composite, and the paper shows safety varies widely at matched capability.
rubric: Prefers o3-mini, citing misalignment safety of 0.99 versus 0.19.
Says capability scores could not distinguish them because their composites are matched (about 0.8).

items.question: A team wants to use LLM coders to assign benchmarks to constructs. Its category definitions were written after the authors saw the results. What residual bias remains, and what kind of evidence does the paper use to address it?
items.answer: Blinding the coders and shuffling options controls coder bias. It does not control rubric-designer bias, because definitions written with the results in view could steer the categories. The paper addresses this with evidence that makes no reference to any criterion: the RQ1 factor, which separates AgentHarm (+0.33) from the R-Judge/InjecAgent cluster.
rubric: Identifies rubric-designer bias as the uncontrolled residual bias.
Says to add criterion-free evidence, such as the RQ1 factor structure separating AgentHarm from R-Judge/InjecAgent.

items.question: A team has a two-scenario misalignment criterion and wants to add a third scenario involving a severe overt harm to improve consistency. What benefit and what cost does the paper's experience suggest?
items.answer: Benefit: a larger battery tightens confidence intervals. In the paper, the interaction p moved from 0.068 to 0.048 with an essentially unchanged point estimate, and the two halves alone agree only moderately (Spearman–Brown 0.70). Cost: a severe overt harm is forecast by harm-compliance measures (AgentHarm → battery +0.43). That dilutes the criterion's construct specificity toward harmful compliance. Adding the scenario post hoc is also a forking path.
rubric: Benefit: greater precision or tighter CIs, given the moderate two-half consistency (SB 0.70) and the p-value drop with an unchanged estimate.
Cost: loss of construct specificity, because severe-harm scenarios track harmful compliance (AgentHarm → battery about +0.43).

items.question: A team will add a benchmark requiring native tool use to a mixed API panel for cross-benchmark correlations. Based on the paper's coverage, what should it expect and plan for?
items.answer: Tool-use benchmarks lose models to malformed tool calls or unsupported routing: AgentHarm reached 19 models and AgentDojo only 5. Such a benchmark will likely cap the common panel, as AgentHarm limited it to n = 18. The team should plan a larger panel, because small panels produce unstable cross-benchmark correlations.
rubric: Expects reduced coverage that limits the common panel, citing AgentHarm (n = 19, common panel 18) and/or AgentDojo (n = 5).
Says to plan for enough models, because small panels give unstable correlations.

items.question: A team builds an organization-level comparison of safety and wants to know which statistical evidence in the paper actually carries organization claims: the within-organization capability slopes or the between-organization permutation test. Which should it rely on, and why?
items.answer: It should rely on the between-organization permutation test on capability-residualized safety ranks. The within-organization slopes rest on only 4–8 models per organization, are sign-heterogeneous, and are distorted by range restriction such as Anthropic's ceiling. The permutation test was also checked for Type-I calibration.
rubric: Chooses the between-organization permutation test.
Reason: within-organization slopes rest on very small n (4–8), vary in sign, and suffer range restriction, while the permutation test was calibration-checked.

items.question: If the specificity–MMLU correlation had stayed near 0.85 at n = 20 instead of falling to +0.16, which RQ2 conclusion would lose its support?
items.answer: The conclusion that the capability confound depends on the reported metric would lose support. Specificity would then be as capability-laden as balanced accuracy (+0.71) and F1 (+0.76). The confound would look like a property of R-Judge as a whole rather than of particular metrics.
rubric: Names the claim that the capability confound is metric-dependent, not a property of the benchmark as a whole.
Reason: all R-Judge metrics, including specificity, would then correlate strongly with capability.

items.question: If both blinded coding rounds had placed the misalignment criterion under risk recognition 7/7, which exploratory result would gain interpretive support, and would it stop being exploratory?
items.answer: The R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment association would gain a construct-matching rationale: risk-recognition predictors would line up with a risk-recognition criterion. It would remain exploratory, because power is about 0.35, it fails Bonferroni, and the pre-specified prediction named AgentHarm.
rubric: Names the R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment association as gaining construct-matching support.
Says it would still be exploratory because of low power, failure of Bonferroni correction, and/or not being the pre-specified prediction.

items.question: If AgentHarm's association with the three-scenario battery had been near zero instead of +0.43, which argument for keeping blackmail+leaking as the primary misalignment criterion would lose force?
items.answer: The construct-dilution argument would lose force. It holds that the murder scenario is a severe harm that harm-compliance measures forecast, so adding it pulls the criterion toward harmful compliance. Without that association, this reason to keep blackmail+leaking primary would weaken. The forking-path concern about a post-hoc addition would remain.
rubric: Identifies the dilution of construct specificity (murder being forecast by harm compliance) as the weakened argument.
Notes that the post-hoc or forking-path objection would still stand.

items.question: If the jailbreak criterion's split-half consistency (resampled by base prompt) had been only about 0.5, would the observed AgentHarm–jailbreak partial of +0.72 be easier or harder to explain, and why?
items.answer: Harder. The paper notes that measurement error attenuates partial relationships instead of inflating them in a predictable direction. A strong +0.72 partial on a criterion that unreliable would be surprising, because noise would cap how large the observed association could be.
rubric: Says the +0.72 would be harder to explain or surprising.
Reason: unreliable measurement attenuates correlations, so a low-consistency criterion would be expected to show a weaker association.

items.question: If Horn's parallel analysis had retained a factor under the Spearman PCA as well, would the paper's treatment of PC1 as corroboration only change?
items.answer: Largely no. One reason for caution, sensitivity to the correlation convention, would be removed. The median between-benchmark correlation would still be only 0.22, though, and the firm RQ1 result would remain the correlation-free ranking disagreement in Table 1. PC1 would still be supporting rather than primary evidence.
rubric: Says the factor would likely still be treated as corroborative.
Reason: the weak median between-benchmark correlation (0.22) remains, and Table 1's disagreement remains the primary RQ1 evidence.

items.question: If misalignment safety had correlated strongly and positively with over-refusal on benign XSTest prompts, which reading of the negative capability–misalignment correlation would gain ground?
items.answer: The reading that less capable models score as 'safer' in the scenario because they refuse or disengage broadly, not because they make better choices about harmful autonomous actions, would gain ground. Part of the crossover's misalignment arm would then reflect blanket refusal rather than safety.
rubric: Names the blanket-refusal or disengagement explanation for why lower-capability models appear safer.
Says this would undermine reading misalignment safety as genuine avoidance of harmful actions.

items.question: Does the paper show that, within a given developer, capability relates to misalignment safety and jailbreak safety in the same direction? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Within Qwen, the capability→safety slope is −0.90 for misalignment but +0.80 for jailbreak, so the directions are opposite. This rests on only n = 5 per organization.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites Qwen's opposite-signed slopes (−0.90 misalignment vs +0.80 jailbreak), optionally noting the small within-organization n.

items.question: Does the paper show that more capable models refuse overtly harmful prompts less often? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Capability's correlation with refusal on XSTest's unsafe subset is −0.32 and not significant. That subset is near ceiling: every model refuses 83–100%, with SD 4.5, which leaves little variance to detect an effect.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Cites the non-significant −0.32 and the ceiling or limited variance of the unsafe subset.

items.question: Does the paper show that the capability–misalignment relationship among the 2026-only models differs from that of the original panel? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The 2026-only models give ρ = +0.07 against the original −0.44, but the independent Fisher z test gives p = 0.12. The nested-bootstrap change (Δρ = +0.27) also has a CI that includes zero.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Cites the non-significant difference tests (Fisher z p = 0.12 and/or a nested-bootstrap CI including zero).

items.question: Do the paper's data show that the lowest-capability models score worst on the audited safety benchmarks? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. In Table 1, Llama-3.1-8B (GPQA 30.4) has the highest AgentHarm safety (0.89). Mistral-Nemo, with the lowest GPQA (28.0), has a high R-Judge specificity of 0.80. Claude-3-Haiku (GPQA 33.3) scores 0.81 on AgentHarm.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites at least one low-capability model that scores high on a safety benchmark (for example Llama-3.1-8B on AgentHarm or Mistral-Nemo on specificity).

items.question: Does the paper show that the capability crossover extends to multi-turn, tool-loop safety outcomes? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The only multi-turn tool-loop criterion is τ² task success. Both safety outcomes, misalignment and jailbreak, are single-turn or scenario-based, so no multi-turn safety outcome was tested.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the safety criteria are single-turn or scenario-based, and only the task-success criterion uses a multi-turn tool loop.

items.question: Does the paper show that the size of AgentHarm's capability-controlled association with jailbreak safety is independent of which jailbreak template is used? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The per-template partials differ substantially: AIM +0.44, refusal-suppression +0.70, prefix-injection +0.62. The single-AIM criterion gives +0.50, against +0.72 for the three-template average.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites the template-dependent partials (for example AIM +0.44 vs refusal-suppression +0.70, or single-AIM +0.50 vs averaged +0.72).

items.question: If the misalignment organization-group permutation p-value were doubled as a worst-case calibration correction, would it still fall below 0.005?
items.answer: No. The misalignment permutation p is 0.004. Doubled, it becomes 0.008, which is above 0.005.
rubric: Answers no.

items.question: If the jailbreak organization-group permutation p-value were doubled as a worst-case calibration correction, would it still fall below 0.005?
items.answer: Yes. The jailbreak permutation p is below 0.001. Doubled, it stays below 0.002, which is under 0.005.
rubric: Answers yes.
Shows that doubling p < 0.001 gives less than 0.002, below 0.005.

items.question: With the positive and negative controls passing, would the pre-specified decision rule permit interpreting the factor structure if PC1 explained 38% of variance but controlling capability reduced the median pairwise partial |ρ| by 0.20?
items.answer: Yes. The rule requires first-factor variance of at least 40% OR a reduction of at least 0.15 from controlling capability, with both controls passing. A 0.20 reduction satisfies the second branch.
rubric: Answers yes.
Reason: the rule is a disjunction, and a reduction of 0.20 meets the at-least-0.15 branch even though variance is below 40%.

items.question: With the positive and negative controls passing, would the pre-specified decision rule permit interpreting the factor structure if PC1 explained 38% of variance and controlling capability reduced the median pairwise partial |ρ| by 0.10?
items.answer: No. Neither branch is met. Variance of 38% falls below the 40% threshold, and a reduction of 0.10 falls below the 0.15 threshold.
rubric: Answers no.
Reason: both conditions fail (38% < 40% and 0.10 < 0.15).

items.question: Would the R-Judge–misalignment partial computed under the classic Pearson-on-rank-residuals convention exceed the minimum detectable effect the paper gives for n = 18?
items.answer: No. Under the classic convention the partial is +0.49, below the minimum detectable effect of 0.62 at n = 18.
rubric: Answers no.
Compares +0.49 with the minimum detectable effect of 0.62.

items.question: Would the AgentHarm–jailbreak partial computed with the swapped (Gemini) refusal grader exceed the minimum detectable effect the paper gives for n = 18?
items.answer: Yes. With the swapped grader the partial is +0.66, above the minimum detectable effect of 0.62.
rubric: Answers yes.
Compares +0.66 with the minimum detectable effect of 0.62.

items.question: In the blinded three-category coding round with a task-success distractor, would the majority of coders place the misalignment criterion in the same construct category as AgentHarm?
items.answer: Yes. In that round the misalignment criterion maps to harm blocking 6/7, the same category AgentHarm receives 7/7.
rubric: Answers yes.
Cites misalignment mapped to harm blocking (6/7), matching AgentHarm.

items.question: In the separate two-way blinded coding round, would the majority of coders place the misalignment criterion in the same construct category as AgentHarm?
items.answer: No. In the two-way round the misalignment criterion maps to risk recognition 6/7, whereas AgentHarm is harm blocking.
rubric: Answers no.
Cites misalignment mapped to risk recognition (6/7), unlike AgentHarm's harm blocking.
